findings.text: The test 'opens no Rust raw string at a raw identifier, nor at a word that ends in r' cannot fail. `r#type` has no `"` after its `#`, so it never opens a fence. In `fooBr#"x"#`, the raw string would close on the same line even without the word check at count.ts:185. Both lines are code either way, so dropping the word check still passes. To exercise it, a line after the `r` must stay inside a string or comment only when the check is missing.

The test 'reads Rust's byte strings, raw ones too, over lines' expects 4 code lines, and every handling gives 4. Without the `br` fence, `br#"first` falls through to an ordinary `"` string, and lines 2–4 are still code. It passes on the code before this change too, so `br`/`b` handling is untested. A comment-looking line inside the `br#"…"#` that counts as code only when the fence is read right would fix this, like the `// in the string` line in the raw-string test.

The test 'reads Rust's strings with escapes, over lines' passes with or without escape handling. If `\"` ended the string, `";` would open another string, and both lines are code anyway. To test that the string continues past `\"`, the next line needs to look like a comment, e.g. `// x`.

The test 'reads Swift's raw strings, where a backslash escapes only with the #s' expects all 5 lines as code. It passes on the code before this change, which knew no `#"` fences, and it would pass if raw strings took `\` as an escape or had no escapes at all. The `\# ` on line 1 only escapes a space. Nothing checks that `#"a\"#` closes at `"#` (a backslash without `#`s escapes nothing), or that `\#"""` keeps a multi-line raw string open where a plain `"""` closer would end it. A line that is comment-like only while the string is still open would make it check this.

blind.summary: I found no code defects. Rust, Swift and Lua are counted as the goal describes. I traced each rule by hand through `fenceAt`, `closeAt`, `CHAR_LITERAL` and the language configs; I did not run the tests. That covers Rust's nested comments, raw and byte strings with any number of `#`, and telling character literals from lifetimes; Swift's nested comments, `"""`, `#"…"#` and `#"""…"""#` with `\#` escapes, and `#if`; and Lua's `--[==[` comments, `[==[` strings and `--[` line comments. The rewritten `closeAt` gives the same results as before for every other language, so they count as they did. What is left are four new tests whose expected counts do not depend on the behaviour they name. Every line in them is code whether the feature works or not, so they pass on the code before this change too.
